blocks.x: Okay, it's going. The microphone's over here, but you can just talk anyplace. Okay.
Yeah, just ignore that.
Yeah, don't worry about that. It'll pick up all over the room.
The name is Frank Adams.
When were you born?
Born in August 1883.
What part of the time? You can just lean back and relax.
And I was born on Dryad Street between 6th and Roysney, right here in New Orleans. And raised out in the Irish Channel.
That's right near where Dave Perkins used to live, huh?

Yeah, near the trombone player. I used to live on Religious Street between Race and Orange once. And we moved from there on Full Street, right near St. Thomas. And we moved from there, we lived on Washington Avenue. Between, let's see, we went to Washington. Well, I had a grown man then. You want that too, from when I'm growing?

I was going to ask a little bit. You say you never played any instrument. You're not a musician. Never played. But you did hear a lot of the bands and were dancers, so that's why we wanted to talk to you.

Now, I danced a lot. I used to go to the hall they called the Love and Charity Hall. Where was that, do you remember? The Love and Charity Hall was on camp, I think, right between Valance and some way up in Alabama.
Yeah, way uptown.
Yeah, uptown.

Now, did your folks, your father play any instrument? Never did. Your mother, was she a singer or anything? No, never was. What was the first music you remember hearing when you were a little boy? Can you remember any? When I was a little boy, it was King Boland.
King Boland. What kind of a band did he have? Well, King Boland used to play a cornet, I think it was. Yeah. Yeah, he used to play a cornet. Called him King Boland.
Remember how big a band he had? Was it a big band, the little women?
Yeah, it was a big band. It was a good size band, I think. He had somewhere around between a dozen men in it.
How did he compare with the other bands?

That, I don't know. But he was tops at that time. Famous. They were white and colored. He was famous at that time. Buddy Boland. We used to call him King Boland. We used to call him King Boland, and his name was Buddy Boland at that time.
Do you know about where he lived?
What part of town? No, I didn't know where Buddy lived, but I knew he lived uptown there somewhere around. Uptown above McCoyland Avenue, around the other way, but whereabouts I didn't know.
What halls? Where else did you go to dances?

No, that was the 11th Shad Hall, and they went to the Globes Hall. Had a hall they called the Globes Hall, and they had a hall they called up on Eagle Street. I can find out to see if I know some other ones. Yeah. Was that? Well, that might have been the one up on Eagle Street. Up on Eagle Street between Poplar and right up in Carrollton there. On the uptown side of the street. Were there any other halls up in Carrollton?
No, not at that time.

The other ones were down on Camp Street. It was right there between Valance and up in there. And then the other one, the Funky Butt Hall was down there. Back around near Basin Street, called the Funky Butt Hall. And they had a hall they called the Economy Hall, but I just remember where the Economy Hall, I think it was down there on the North Line, see.
Yeah, I think it's old Irsalon.

Yeah, I think it's old Irsalon. Yeah. The other ones were there with stuff there with balancing up in there and then the other one the funky butthole was down there back around near Basin Street called the funky butthole and they had a hall they called economy hall but I just remember where the economy hall economy hall I think was down there on the North Line see yeah I think it's
old Ursuline yeah it's still there it's a church there yeah yeah I think it's down there

do you remember remember Masonic Hall oh yeah where was that the old Masonic Hall well let me see where was it located in that old Masonic Hall if I can remember right I can soon find it out sometimes because I know other friends of mine that too they memorize and where it was at if you have
some other friends that way you can get them to talk on tape someday too I have some older men that

knew they're older than men the oldest men older there's no a bold and some of those people used to play music too now I know one guy used to play music he's a main guy he can tell you about all them halls I guess pretty much remember his name now yeah one of them died was two brothers of them was a barber in barber business and used to play music but one of them died Joe died last year year before last and the other brothers up here now at the barber shop on force and liberty oh we know him John Joseph yeah we know him yes we know him you know the right people yeah tell us about him oh go ahead let me see and who else yeah and then he had a brother a younger brother but he died some years ago too the same Joe the clarinet player yeah he died too I knew him uh and then let's see who else and then there was uh well well Buddy Bartley he wasn't a musician but he used to go in the uh at Lincoln Park they used to call it and then they don't come back on them and they'd be uh grocery back there on the place right now because he used to be a great big place and uh Buddy Bartley used to go up in the balloon you know and everybody used to go out there and go up in the balloon out at Lincoln Park yeah Lincoln Park did you go out there did they have any dancing or yeah dancing out there Lincoln Park would they have the band playing while he went up in the balloon yeah Buddy Bowling used to be out there too right well would they play any special tune when he went up in the balloon or well no but most of the things they'd be dancing looking
at him going up in the balloon all of that you know did you ever see sunshine money go up in the balloon

no that was a tale too they say but I never see him say he got up there and they sit all the way oh they sang that song about him you know that bill no I don't know sunshine money was a hollow man I know sunshine money well he died yeah he's a preacher he died his wife is right back on church he's there now she lives third and what third between 20 somewhere around I know where the house was I forget his wife is right there now she ain't moved since I seen her there's no sunshine money and then uh let's see and they had another guy famous musician who was that again uh Buddy Bowling and this Joseph and then several more I knew of this and I had to present so I jumped up in the heart to see if I knew that I could figure back well we'll see you another day you know yeah you come back ready again I remember I was way back there when I can think it over just like I told about that now I was going to ask about down in the Irish Channel you said when you were raised there oh yeah but that fight but that um what about the uh
you say some of the white people you told me that treated you very nice some oh yeah oh yeah that was

the stacks 80 stacks and Walter Stakes 80 he's he's an engineer for the town pickagoon right now he's about my height but the heavier than me black half last time I heard him he's right there at the time picking him into that I guess he's there yeah but the white and colored got along pretty well most of the time there right in the channel we played together we had together in this house he had but he had more than my mother's house and I had in this house because my mother would always have our dinner ready or breakfast and beat her mother cooking see and pies and cakes that go around the corner at the Saffirou market on Saffirou street we lived in that was on first between Russo and Chapatula at that time and they'd go around the corner at the market called Saffirou market around there and you used to buy all the meats and stuff and the vegetables like the cabbage and the uh parsley and the onions and green onion and all where that playground is now huh huh where that playground is now oh and Saffirou got playground in there yeah I think so around Chapatula's uh well Borussia's baker shops out that way too oh yeah so anyway they go around that way and buy all the meats and come to my mother and they'd get their vegetable stuff right out of the garden fresh they'd carry everything else and ask my mother how much of my mother would take a penny then tomatoes and everything and my dad used to plant all that stuff and had great big frontier all from here way little deep and across the street and they fixed all that great big garden corn and everything there was two grains of corn and everything and they come right there and load up the basket get all it was right in between all the white neighbors they had only two colored families in that block at that time uh the uh uh what was the other people's name well let's see now the Anderson's they lived right near the corner and we lived in between Chapatula's and Russo but we right next to us in between more than they were
did you know a fellow named Joey Sales up there he was a guitar player?
Joey Sales?
Sales Sales he lived in the channel I think he used to work with Robichaux's band I'm trying to remember
I remember Robichaux too I forgot about him Robichaux yeah Robichaux was famous did you dance to him? yeah yeah Robichaux was famous that was that was a big band they were
what were they like?
well
did they did they play as uh low down music as Bolden?
yeah they played low down music as Bolden?
oh yeah and Bolden would he play strictly Gut Bucket low down or would he play upper class refined?
well he plays the old bell house music oh yeah Robichaux oh yeah Robichaux old dance way back then
what kind of dances did you like in those days?

what kind of dances did you like? well there was the chord drill at that time the chord drill and the two-step and the and the and the and the shallots and all that at that time you mentioned the mazooka too before yeah yeah mazooka too how'd that yeah one was used to dance and dance and uh and then they used to have another dance what they call that again oh what was that again mmm what's your color did they have any waltzes in those days? yeah waltzes too yeah they used to waltz what was the other one you were thinking of? I'm trying to think now the waltz the two-step mazooka and the shallots and the shallots I forget the other ones I used to dance all the most
did they have play many blues in those days? yeah plenty blues that's what the blues did
the time when they used to play the blues
did they do them slow or fast how did they like to rock and roll fast or slow?
they didn't take them fast or take them slow either way but that means they used to play that's all they used to play
do you remember any particular ones that were famous?
not that now since I put all that down a long years ago and there was always never even looked back there I went to join church and I never even looked like that
yeah oh yeah do you remember the slow drag dance was that a dance?
yes slow drag had the old slow drag too
where was that popular? any particular hall famous?
no in all the halls
they did the same dances in all the halls? in all the halls would they dance righty when they danced in quadrille?
no quadrille wasn't righty
what was righty in the way of dancing?
well that uh that's let me see what what you call that thing that oh not the dip had a dance called the dip too you remember? the dip
I remember that before my time

yeah dip you know you see oh lord if I could sit down here and take my pocket if I knew that I could have been taking over I guess I could have given a lot more of it but I'd put it down so long you go and never even look back at that the way I'd such things like that
yeah
young and foolish you know
you mentioned you were a pretty good dancer were you?
yeah I was at that time
the girls liked to dance with you oh yeah you told me

any hall they knew I was at they'd be there unless the boys would get angry with me and everything else wanted to fight me and jump on me but they knew if they helped me they had to fight that's all we'd fight but fire fish we didn't cut nobody shoot nobody we used to fight fire fish you're a better man than I was well they just separated from that's all we'd make shake hands make friends and take a drink or two and that's all
oh you've uh told me before about yeah each fella had a friend they had to fight and they did

yeah that's like you and him and I had my other friend of me and him and my friend want to fight and your friend want to fight my friend well all right well then we'd like to we'd see if they had a knife and thing else and then now make them go out there and see and go fight now nobody jump at all now either one that Holly got enough then we'd make him try and let you look and make him shake hands that's the way we used to
uh can you tell us about that the Robert Charles riot

oh Robert Charles riot yeah that's what happened on I think it was on Saratoga between the Irada and and Clio somewhere around the other on the the woods side of the street like the cafe over there like the rich cafe and uh he was waiting for his wife and so they said and police ran up there and the colored woman went and called the police and said he was standing around there so long she didn't know what he's waiting around there for and what come to find out the man was waiting for his wife to see his wife and he said what he gonna kill her or what he was waiting to see her wasn't about nobody and officers came on up there and called him black s p what you're doing around here yeah the man said now listen don't have a meet out of the way he said uh um why don't you ask me what i want what i'm doing around here perhaps i might tell you and who you talking to he said i'm talking to you ain't you a man like me you're talking to me and they didn't like that and then they started down to get his gun when they started down to get his gun this guy
The police started for their guns? Yeah, they started for their guns first.
So then Robert Sarle pulled out his guns?
Robert Sarle pulled out his guns, put it on the quick. And as he put it on him, well the other one right, put it on that one. He's gone, he put it on four of them.
And he was gone. He got about four of them right there. Right there. Gone.
The whole city came in to see about it. I don't remember that good.
Did you have another song about Robert Charles?
I used to sing about it, but I don't remember. Well you told me a little bit more before about Robert Charles. He went upstairs? Oh yeah.

Yeah, they got in behind him then and he made it across the way and went upstairs in an old house. And when he went up in the old house, then he had all of them in front of him. See, and everyone tried to come up there and break in. And he seen him, he put it on him. He had it on them, he put it on him. See? Shot everyone up as they came up the stairs. Yeah, they come up as they tried to come up. Yeah. He put it on them. And then they tried to set the house on fine. He said no, they better not because they burned down people's house. In order to make them run out so they could get it. So then they went all around surrounding the house and tried to climb up and try to get it. And everyone he seen by the way and put it on him. Boom.
Shot him every direction. Then he got away. How did he get away?
I was told he got away by night. In clothes. I don't know. I never seen him, but that's what I heard him say. Then he got away by night.
Did you say somebody dressed him, you told me he dressed him in women's clothes maybe? In women's clothes.
That's what I was telling you. Somebody told you about it. Out of the way. He was a mason and a heart fell and everything.
Did you know Robert Charles personally?
No, no, I didn't know anybody. You just heard about it. Just heard about it.
I've heard that he was a very nice, quiet kind of fellow and wouldn't cause anybody any trouble until that came up.

That's what I said. Tell him this came up. That's what it said. That's what the man said that he was talking for. Even though it was a police. He started handling him rough, you know. And I just started to do him. Want to hit you. Want to beat you up. But I waited for him to know anything about it. What's what?
Some of them. Not all of them.
What went on?
Did you ever hear where he died? What happened to him? No, I heard he died in Chicago.
Whereabouts in Chicago? Well, what about the riot that was going on? That was the riot then.
Yeah, but I mean the other stuff.

Oh yeah, then the other white people began then to all around the house, they said we were going to kill up a lot of colored folks on the ground. That riot, you see, was the police on them. And doing that to Mr. Stacks, the same boy, I tell you I know this one, probably his dad. He lived next door to us. Come and warn my dad and told him that some hoodlums going to form up a gang and come all around and kill all the colored folks. On account of that riot. We didn't know nothing about them. We were way out in front of that. We were way back in town here. We were nowhere around. We didn't know nothing about them. We don't know what we heard. Yeah. We were way out of that. And so, anyway, Mr. Stacks come and notified my dad and asked him, say, no, I don't trust him. Listen, I told my wife who got to bed, say, you and your madam are going to sleep in my bed. That's where me and my madam sleep in. And Frank, that's me, and my other brother next to me was in Chicago now, my younger brother, I'm going to sleep in the bed with Walter and Eddie. Eddie's up there, but Walter died. He said, I was the younger brother, died. Only Eddie's living. And so, I told my dad, and so my dad, he said, no. He says, uh, I said, Stacks, I thank you ever so much. But he says, no, he says, I'd be less than a man who leave my house to go in your house. He said, you know, I don't bother nobody. I never did. He said, no, I know you didn't. He said, but Adam, you going to stay around there? He says, I'm going to walk the street all night long with his shotgun. He said, and he going to tell them, none of them stop in this block to harm any one of you couples. The dude is going to have to kill me all my day. At least he'll have to die. Because he ain't going to take back and say he's going to kill him. And then he'll have to kill him. And he said, he'd rather die right there until he's going to fight for him. He ain't going to let nobody stop in that block to battle those kind of people at all.
He's a good friend of yours. Oh yeah.
Nice friend. So then my daddy, he asked my daddy, he said, well, what you going to do about it? Hold just a second.
Hold just a second. Here we go.
We'll have another chair, Bill. All right.
You were telling us about your neighbors and all up there at the time of that riot. Uh-huh. And so, my dad told Mrs. Sacks, no, I'm not going to leave my house.

He said, well, Adam, what you going to do? He said, of course, I'm going to fight. He said, I'm fighting until they kill me. I said, I'm going to fight for you all. be safe? Now, we the owners went in there, but the other colored folks were down in there, but he's going to protect them, but we the owners went in his house. Some of the white neighbors invited them to go over to their house.
They were going to shoot all the colored people in the neighborhood.

Yeah. And some of them are ours hoodlums, you know. Yeah. So, my dad said, no. So, I said, what you going to do? He said, well, he said, have you got anything to protect yourself? He said, well, I'll show you. I got this little thing. Show him a shotgun and a big .45. You know, kid, like you couldn't go and look at the old people to see what they're doing, like you're killing anybody now. He said, my father has a big .45 on the shotgun. I didn't know he had it myself. So, he had that and he told him, he said, you got plenty of ammunition. He said, now I'll help you entertain them if they come. Did anybody bother you? No, wait a minute. So, he said, now I'm going to tell you what we going to do, Mr. Stacks or my daddy said, now I'm going to stand on the Chapel Tula Street. And when they started coming, he said, I'm going to stop them and tell them, now look, don't you know, go nowhere around here and buy none of these colored people around here. If you do, you're going to have to bother with them over my dead body, because I ain't going to stand for it. And they told my daddy, he said, now I'm going to notify you. He said, if they're going to come in anyhow, going to come down the block anyhow, I'm going to make one shot up in the air. And you see, then he'd be behind them and my daddy got them in front. And they started hitting the thing, they couldn't go back and they couldn't go front. My daddy and him boy would have them covered, you see. My daddy had the .45 Andy Shack. And he had his big shot. So, when they, they listened to what he said, and they didn't stop nowhere in my block, but he went right around the corner, and an old colored woman, been paralyzed in the chair for years and years, ever since I was getting older. And sitting at the door in the summertime too, you know, and I believe she had to add something else to, to catch air, you know. And went right around there and killed that old lady. Killed her right there.
Well they would choose a defenseless old woman.
Broke up the chair and killed the old woman. Now what that old lady had to do?
Yeah, nothing. She didn't even know there was a riot. Didn't know nothing about it. Didn't know anything about it.
Didn't know anything about it.
How were the Irish people in general in your neighborhood? Were they a tough bunch? Oh yeah, it was tough.

They'd always be fighting and drunk amongst themselves and fight with, and they worked right on the river, on the river front, which is. And in the evening, sometime they get half drunk, you pass by later, they didn't know you anymore, nobody else. And unless you had to scrap with them, if you scrap with them and fight them, and then they know you wasn't going to run, then you and them were good friends, and they look around, well that's Adam. He is out pat, oh, what's Adam? All right, pat you on the back and you going by. Now let some other colored poison pass that other way. They'll hop by them and beat your brains. Now, if you run up there and say, hold up, say don't hit that bar, don't it? I know them, well, the good friends of my internment was leaving alone, pull them away from them, and they know you're going to scrap, and then you're going to let them alone. They're going to kind of leave. But you had to fight them though. You survived them though. You fight for half of these weeds, you survived them though. But the Irishmen, you know, you bleed, you fight them, you know, and you hit them in the mouth of them, you know, and the more they bleed, the more they're coming on you. But you have the weapon, you have the children, you can fight, and I had to fight them too. Now they survived them. My brother, now next to me was heavy, heavy, a whole lot heavier than me, and muscles and everything else. But if he wouldn't fight, he would want to run, see. So, after when he did get to fighting, I told my dad, my daddy whipped him several times by and told me he'd better fight, stand there with me and fight. Don't you go pick no trouble, but don't you run. If you get whipped, you stand there and fight. And Frank, you let me know if he run. I said, I will. When he did start the fight and he hit, when he hit, he would have to go against that pole somewhere. When he did start the fight and he was tough, I had to stop him from fighting. When he did start, yeah. He'd be girls and boys and everybody for nothing, but I would have to stop him, you see. But I never bothered nobody. I never did. Never always liked friends. Always from a boy. Never would mess with nobody. But now if you hopped on me and give me friends, then we gonna fight. But I didn't look for you. You gonna fight, man. I ain't gonna run. And I know you don't want to get beat up no more than me, and you somebody gonna holler. See, when you fight, then they shake hands and they see, well, you're all a pal, then they ain't gonna fight you no more cause you know you gonna fight with them. But now if you run, if you run, they gonna keep you running. See, they fight themselves. Now about this boy, Poesie, man. Poesie, man. Poesie, man. He was up there, around there, and I was living then on, where was I living then? Not far from there. On Melfermean, see, I was married then. Got married. On Melfermean between Car and Willa. But more near Willa next to the Italian grocery named Charlie. Charlie Prestigiacomo, he's right there, yeah. And after a while we seen a guy running towards Magnolia Street. Well, I never did run to go look to see what's happening. But I happened to be going out, going out somewhere, and I come on out that thing, going up Magnolia Street, and they had the crisis gathering, you know. And they had this boy, Poesie, in jail. They didn't want to go beating on him, you know, everything else, and all that they was beating him all up and everything else. But what, I don't know, the policemen was. That's the way they do them when they get them up there at 12. They beat their brains out of them all. Nobody wouldn't stop them. And so they was beating Poesie, so Poesie being a good young man, he punched him. The one would hit him and punched him, knocked him down. When he knocked him down, and before he could get up, he was reaching over for his gun, and Poesie grabbed the gun, beat him, got the gun from him, and the other one wanted to shoot Poesie. And when they did, Poesie put down the power of him. That's what I was told. Then they started shooting and shooting and shooting. The whole force was around at the 12th precinct, and they all tried to get the boy, they had him in jail already. And the captain wanted to send them up there to go there, see if they could get Poesie to surrender to them, and tell them to give them a fire trial and all, and don't shoot no more, and give the gun up and come on and surrender. So this one wanted to go, and the other one wanted to go, and neither one of them wanted to go up there.
Was that right in the jailhouse? Right in the jailhouse.

They had the boy in the jailhouse already in the cell. Yeah. See, and that's where they struck that little buck beating the boy up. And so then they had a fire engine house around there, see, on that side. Then in the back of the jail, they had a, on this side, on McNordy's side, they had a fire engine house, had a shed, trapped shed, and they was getting on that shed and everything else, and Poesie seen them, you know, through the, through the bars, and he'd put it on, everyone would get up on top of that shed, he'd let them get almost up to the bars, almost, and he'd drive and you could see why they'd fall, and instead of falling back, they'd fall in front. Some fell back, you know, and he bumped them.
How many guns did he have?
Only that one gun he'd taken. He'd taken that one gun, then after he used that out, he killed three or four of them. Then he had the other guns right there by him, see.
I wondered how he had all that ammunition to keep it going.
He had that right there by him, see. That's what I was told.
Did he get out of jail then? No.

So anyway, so I was told now, they'd like to have a riot then again, on the kind of pushing them, see. So they're making everybody get back, he couldn't go see. Well, I didn't want to see, I just passed by there, and the time on that side when I seen all and hear about what it was all about, and I stood at the next second corner and heard about what it was, and I kept on going. I said, I didn't want to get no straight shots, even if somebody else was me. I never did run up to a crowd or get away from a crowd, always did. So anyway, and going, then I heard that after I got away and all, and all said, they got Persia to surrender. And after they got him to surrender to the chief, the chief made them all get back, and he went on up there and begged for it, and so the poor friend, look, I ain't got my weapon, I left my gun downstairs and all, now just surrender to me, and I'll be your friend, and I see that you get a fat saw. So Persia taking him out of his wood, and after Persia gave the gun up and gave it, and they put him in the automobile, in the patrol, in the car, wagon somewhere, and taking the way out somewhere on the highway somewhere, and they all shot him all up. Probably did. Killed the police. Never got no child, just killed him all up. Mm-hmm.

Yeah, I heard that about one, maybe the same fellow, George Lewis told me. Yeah. There was another riot, Seymour or somebody, did you ever hear of that one, Sheik? No. Bunk told me about it. You heard of the Persia one. I mean, that ain't been too long. No.
About 20 years. Seymour, I don't remember after Seymour. The Persia was about 20 years ago.
Oh, yeah. I mean, that ain't been too long.
No. About 20 years. About 20 years ago.
Oh, more long than that. Oh, I was mad.
Oh, that's way longer than 20 years.
When were you born, 1908? There's only another minute on here, so is there anything else?
I don't know. I don't know.
I don't know. I don't know. I don't know.
tell us about the bands you heard any what about parades do you remember any
of the big parades when you were a boy? Yeah the carnival parade and the king and the queen and all of that and the wrecks, the wrecks parade. Do you remember any of the colored
organizations like the lodges and the ones uptown what kind of parades did they have were they on Sunday afternoons those kind of parades I mean? Well they had a

fellow here by the name what's his name used to work for D. H. Holmes used to put on parades and things I forget his name again he lived on Second Street he died oh about 10 to 12 years ago more he lived on Second Street and he used to have parades and all during the carnival time they used to put on parades and everything else and pass on Canal Street and stuff at home did that where he worked at and

learned with the floats and all the air floats and different. Now can you tell me do you remember when you were a little boy did they have the funerals with the brass band on the funerals when you were really a little kid maybe eight or nine years old can you remember that? Yeah with the brass bands

brass bands and uh they had old time horses with the horses with the black uh I don't know what you call it all draped down over the horses you know like a mosquito ball all black you know knitted work all the time of the horses had the old brass lamps on each side of the horse old time just like you see me in that cell and now. Did they have a brass band with them too? Yeah brass band. Brass band. Did you ever follow those uh funerals go to the graveyard and come back with them or anything? Never did. Never did. Never did like that. Never did in my life. Because they played jazz I heard. They played jazz and they'd be dancing in the street behind the cops and I look at them. I never did. Didn't do that? Never did. I had more respect for the dead than that. But some of them didn't have no more sense and that they're too lively wouldn't they? That's all we got.

segments.title: Setting up the recording
segments.summary: Interviewer checks the microphone and Frank Adams is told to talk freely.

segments.title: Frank Adams's birth and boyhood homes in the Irish Channel
segments.summary: Adams gives his name, an August 1883 birth on Dryad Street, and the streets he lived on while growing up.

segments.title: Adams the dancer, not a musician; Love and Charity Hall
segments.summary: Interviewer notes Adams never played an instrument but heard bands and danced; he places the Love and Charity Hall uptown.

segments.title: First music remembered: Buddy 'King' Boland's band
segments.summary: Adams recalls King Boland, a cornetist with a dozen-piece band, famous among white and colored audiences.

segments.title: Dance halls: Globe, Funky Butt, Economy Hall, Masonic Hall
segments.summary: Adams lists halls where he danced, on Camp, Eagle, near Basin Street and North Line, as he and the interviewers sort out locations.

segments.title: Older musician friends, Lincoln Park balloon ascents and Sunshine Money
segments.summary: Adams names barber-musician brothers, Buddy Bartley's balloon rides at Lincoln Park with dancing, and Sunshine Money, now deceased.

segments.title: Mixed neighborhood in the Irish Channel and the Saffiro market
segments.summary: White and colored neighbors got along; Adams describes the Stacks family, the market, and his father's garden.

segments.title: Robichaux's and Bolden's bands and their low-down music
segments.summary: Kid Sheik asks about Joey Sales, Robichaux and Bolden; Adams says they played the same low-down dance music.

segments.title: Dances of the day, blues and the slow drag
segments.summary: Adams names quadrille, two-step, mazurka, schottische, waltz, slow drag and the dip, and says blues were played plenty.

segments.title: Being a good dancer and the fistfights at halls
segments.summary: Adams says girls liked dancing with him and describes fair fistfights between friends that ended in handshakes.

segments.title: The Robert Charles shootout and his escape
segments.summary: Adams tells how police confronted Robert Charles waiting for his wife, shots followed, and he fled upstairs and escaped.

segments.title: Whether Adams knew Robert Charles; what became of him
segments.summary: Adams only heard about him; Kid Sheik says he was quiet; the interviewer heard he died in Chicago.

segments.title: Mr. Stacks warns Adams's family of a white mob
segments.summary: Neighbor Stacks warns that hoodlums will attack colored families and offers his bed; Adams's father refuses to leave his house.

segments.title: Adams's father arms himself; an old woman is killed
segments.summary: Adams's father shows a shotgun and .45 and plans to hold the block; the mob goes around the corner and kills a paralyzed old woman.

segments.chapter: Irish Channel and the Poesie shooting
segments.title: Fighting the Irish; the start of the Poesie jailhouse shooting
segments.summary: Adams explains how standing up to Irish dockworkers earned respect, then begins the story of Poesie beaten by police at the 12th precinct.

segments.chapter: Irish Channel and the Poesie shooting
segments.title: Poesie's stand in the jail and his surrender and killing
segments.summary: Adams relates how Poesie shot at police from his cell, then surrendered to the chief and was reportedly shot.

segments.chapter: Irish Channel and the Poesie shooting
segments.title: Dating the Persia and other riots; tape nearly out
segments.summary: Interviewers compare this with other riots they heard of and argue how long ago it was before the tape ends.

segments.title: Carnival and lodge parades
segments.summary: Adams recalls carnival parades, the king and queen, and a man who staged parades on Canal Street.

segments.title: Brass bands at funerals
segments.summary: Adams describes draped horses and brass bands at funerals but never followed them out of respect.
